findings.title: CSS gets the classes present in the evaluation frames, but the paper and the baselines.py docstring say it gets the full vocabulary
findings.where: papers/main.tex:643-644 (setup, 'Segmentation baselines'); usplat/baselines.py:33-37 (docstring (d)) and :336-337 (CSS.__init__ docstring); scripts/run_mapping.py:104-120 (css_vocabulary); scripts/replica_tab1.sh (--css-eval-data $ROOT/$s/Sequence_2)
findings.problem: The code decides which is true. run_mapping.css_vocabulary builds the CSS label set from the GT label maps of Sequence_2 (the evaluation frames) and keeps only the classes present there. The paper says 'CSS receives the full vocabulary at mapping time, which the open-vocabulary rows do not need'. The baselines.py docstring says CSS gets 'configs/vocab_replica.json, all classes ... never the classes present in a test scene'. Both statements are false. CSS actually receives 16-28 classes, taken from the evaluation GT. That is exactly the query set every other row gets at query time. So CSS is not handicapped by 100 classes at mapping time. It has the same class information as the other rows, only earlier. The class count K also sets how strong CSS's flat Dirichlet prior is (see the next finding), so the stated protocol would give different CSS numbers.
findings.failure_scenario: The test run as scripted maps every test scene with the present-class CSS. Table I then prints CSS numbers (on val so far the best ECE, 4.65 vs 7.05 for ours P2) under a text that describes a harder protocol. A reader or reviewer would credit CSS's calibration to a full-vocabulary setting it never ran. If the authors instead decide after the test run that CSS should get the full vocabulary, they must re-map and re-evaluate the test scenes. CSS counts are built at mapping time, so that means a second test run.
findings.evidence:
CPU script (scratchpad/present.py) compares css_vocabulary() with eval_seg's present-query rule (load_frames + torch.unique) for all 8 scenes:
  office_0 eval K 24 css K 24 css-only [] eval-only [] same order True
  room_2 eval K 21 css K 21 ... True
  room_0 28/28, room_1 24/24, office_1 22/22, office_2 21/21, office_3 26/26, office_4 16/16, all identical ids and order.
The saved field agrees: torch.load(office_0_lseg.pt)['css_class_ids'] = [10, 12, 17, 20, 22, 31, 35, 37, 40, 44, 47, 56, 60, 63, 76, 79, 80, 82, 83, 87, 92, 93, 95, 98] (24 of 101). map_office_0.log reads 'CSS vocabulary: 24 classes present in .../office_0/Sequence_2' and map_room_2.log reads '21 classes'. main.tex:643: 'CSS receives the full vocabulary at mapping time, which the open-vocabulary rows do not need.' The run report README line 17 says it correctly: 'CSS (Dirichlet over the present classes, given at mapping time)'.
findings.fix: Decide before STAGE=test. The cheap option keeps the code and fixes the text. main.tex:643-644 would read: 'CSS receives at mapping time the classes present in the scene's evaluation frames (16 to 28 classes), the same set that every row is queried with. CSS's own Replica experiments also use a scene-level closed set.' Also fix baselines.py docstring (d) and the CSS.__init__ docstring to say the same. Only if a full-vocabulary CSS is wanted: change css_vocabulary to use all non-ignored vocab ids, then re-map the val scenes and refit the val betas before any test run.

findings.title: CSS's flat prior alpha0 = 1 is unstated and untuned, yet it is about 26-28% of the mass-weighted Dirichlet mean and likely drives CSS's ECE lead
findings.where: usplat/baselines.py:334-339 (alpha0=1.0, docstring '[A: fixed on val]'); usplat/baselines.py:526 (default_baselines alpha0=1.0); papers/main.tex:641-646 (no prior stated)
findings.problem: CSS's row buffer is the Dirichlet mean (counts + alpha0)/(sum counts + K*alpha0). The counts are pixel masses at the 240x320 mapping resolution, and most Gaussians are tiny (median 4.2 px total mass in office_0, 1.5 px in room_2). So the flat prior K*alpha0 = K is large next to the evidence. The CSS predictive is therefore a probability mixture with strong, evidence-dependent smoothing toward uniform. That is a plausible cause of its val calibration lead (ECE 4.65, NLL 0.956 vs averaging 7.40 / 1.065 and ours P2 7.05 / 1.055). It is a real property of this CSS configuration, not a bug. I checked the other candidate artefacts: the tie rule, coverage, the temperature-fit procedure and the class-column selection all treat probs and feature rows alike. But the size of the effect is set by three unstated choices: alpha0 = 1, K = the number of present classes, and the mapping resolution. The docstring tag '[A: fixed on val]' is not backed by any val selection; the reports have no alpha0 search and the value is the constructor default.
findings.failure_scenario: The paper reports CSS as the best-calibrated row, or tries to explain why P1/P2 lose to it on ECE/NLL, without saying that CSS's predictive is about 27% uniform prior by mass. A reader cannot reproduce the CSS row, because neither alpha0 nor K is given. With the full vocabulary the paper describes (K = 101), the prior share would roughly double, so the stated setup would give a different CSS ECE.
findings.evidence:
CPU script (scratchpad/css_state.py) on the saved val fields:
 office_0: K 24 alpha0 1.0; per-Gaussian CSS mass quantiles q10..q99 = [0.15, 0.72, 4.18, 20.2, 59.1, 256]; 'mass-weighted prior share of the Dirichlet mean: 0.278'; 'same with K=101: 0.533'; CSS total counts = NormLift S1 (max abs diff 1e-3).
 room_2: K 21; prior share 0.258; with K=101: 0.505.
Partial val (logs/eval_val_partial_2013.log): css ECE 0.0465 NLL 0.9563, fitted beta 1.32 (sharpening on log q, which offsets part of the smoothing); averaging ECE 0.0740 NLL 1.0653; ours_P2 ECE 0.0705 NLL 1.0549.
`grep -rn alpha0 docs/reports/2026-09-29-data-and-baselines/ docs/reports/2026-09-29-paper-revision-1/logs/fact_sheet.md papers/main.tex` returns nothing.
findings.fix: State it in the setup: 'CSS uses a flat Dirichlet prior, alpha_0 = 1 per class, over the K present classes, with counts in pixels at 240x320.' Replace '[A: fixed on val]' in the docstring with 'default, not tuned'. Optionally, before the test run, pick alpha0 on the val scenes with a small grid (e.g. 0.01, 0.1, 1). alpha0 enters only at read-out (alpha = counts + alpha0), so this needs no re-mapping, only a CSS config override at load. When the results are interpreted, say that CSS's calibration comes from probability averaging plus prior smoothing.

findings.title: The AUSE_u column ranks pixels with undefined u_ale as most uncertain, which gives our row a support signal the baseline channels do not get; the paper does not say this
findings.where: usplat/seg_eval.py:338-362 (undefined_key / ranking_signals: NaN u ranked above every finite value); scripts/make_tables.py:22-28 (ours AUSE_u = u_ale; NormLift 1-R, 1-C_inter and CSS css_var_top are always finite); papers/main.tex:680-682 (metrics text mentions only uncovered pixels) and caption of tab:replica
findings.problem: In Table I, AUSE_u compares ours' u_ale with NormLift's 1-R and 1-C_inter and with CSS's variance, all against the 0/1 error. A pixel's u_ale is undefined (NaN) when more than half its alpha comes from Gaussians with support < tau_min = 3 weighted views. ranking_signals puts those pixels in a tier above every defined value. That tier is a few-views (epistemic) signal, and it enters ours' 'aleatoric' column. The baseline channels are finite everywhere, so they get no such tier. The defined u_ale values are also tiny and flat, so the NaN tier may carry much of ours' ranking. The paper does compare rho_hat with C_inter 'at few views', but in this metric ours never gets scored in the few-views regime: it is set to 'most uncertain' instead.
findings.failure_scenario: Ours' AUSE_u beats 1-C_inter or the CSS variance partly because of which pixels have fewer than 3 weighted views, not because rho_hat is a better aleatoric estimator. The table and text would credit the estimator. The same tier also feeds the u_ale vs e_irr panel of the views figure.
findings.evidence:
CPU script (scratchpad/tiers.py) on the saved fields:
 office_0: 'pixel-mass share: u_ale undefined 0.158 | 1-C_inter == 0 (C_inter=1) 5.1e-07'; u_ale defined q50/q90/q99/max = 0.017/0.043/0.058/0.101
 room_2: 'u_ale undefined 0.182 | 1-C_inter == 0 1.7e-06'; u_ale defined q50/q90/q99/max = 0.003/0.019/0.039/0.089
(consistent with logs/support_stats.log: u_ale defined for 84.2% / 81.8% of pixel mass).
seg_eval.py:360: key = torch.where(isfinite(u), u, undefined_key(u)), i.e. NaN ranks above max finite u. main.tex:681-682 states the most-uncertain rule only for uncovered pixels.
findings.fix: State the rule in the metrics text and the Table I caption: 'pixels where u_ale is undefined (fewer than tau_min views) rank as most uncertain; X% of covered pixels'. n_undefined is already in the JSON. Also report ours' u_ale AUSE on the pixels where it is defined (covered and defined), or give the baseline channels the same treatment (undefined where the NormLift N_eff or CSS support is below the same threshold). Then the column compares estimators on the same pixels.

findings.title: The 2D row covers every pixel, while the 3D rows count their uncovered pixels as wrong; the paper does not say this
findings.problem: The 2D row's rasterizer returns alpha = 1 for every pixel, so all labelled pixels count as covered. The 3D rows lose about 0.3% of pixels to the coverage rule. Those pixels are counted wrong and get the uniform predictive in the 'all' variant. The metrics text defines coverage through the 'rendered opacity', which the 2D row does not have.
findings.failure_scenario: The 2D vs 3D accuracy gap in Table I includes up to about 0.3 points that come from coverage, not semantics. The effect is small but not stated.
findings.evidence: eval_val_partial_2013.log: office_0 2d_features coverage 1.000; all 3D rows coverage 0.997.
findings.fix: Add one clause to the setup: '2D features cover every pixel; a 3D row's pixels with alpha_p < tau_cov count as wrong (0.3% on validation)'. Or also report the 'covered' variant for the 3D rows.

findings.title: A stale LaTeX comment says normlift_1-Cinter is not exposed
findings.problem: The comment says 'usplat/baselines.py defines c_inter() but uncertainties() exposes only normlift_1-R and normlift_epi. Expose normlift_1-Cinter before this row runs.' Commit 4829617 added that channel (baselines.py:246), and make_tables.py reads it.
findings.failure_scenario: A later editor or reviewer trusts the comment and thinks the 1 - C_inter row of Table I cannot have been measured.
findings.evidence: baselines.py:243-246 returns 'normlift_1-Cinter'; tests/test_baselines.py:147-149 checks it; on office_0 it is finite, range [-2.4e-7, 1.0].

checked_ok: tests/test_baselines.py: 13 passed on CPU (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests/test_baselines.py).

NormLift code (baselines.py:192-251) matches arXiv 2609.18898 Sec. 3.3 as fetched: W = sum_i A_ij; f^(v) = sum A B / W; f_j is weight-normalized, not unit; C_intra and C_inter as Eq. 7; N_eff = (sum W)^2 / sum W^2 over the per-view rendering weights; R = ||f|| N_eff / (N_eff + beta) with beta = 1; query u* = f/||f||; CLIP inputs unit-norm. Our z is unit: upsample_tokens normalizes and pca.project renormalizes. Paper setup text (main.tex:633-641) describes it correctly, including 'without its KNN voting refinement'.

CSS equation references match arXiv 2411.02547: Eq. 12 kernel-weighted count update, Eq. 15 squared-weight variance compositing, Eq. 18 expectation measure. The paper states the linear-weight compositing change. CSS's own Replica runs also use a scene-level closed set (28 classes) with LSeg labels.
The CSS vocabulary equals the eval query set (same ids, same order) in all 8 scenes, so CSS.columns() cannot raise in the test run.
CSS and the field see the same pixels and weights: CSS total counts equal NormLift S1 to 1e-3 on office_0, and both leave the same share of Gaussians unseen (2.49% office_0, 4.65% room_2).

The run_mapping.py token pre-extraction is equivalent to 60d7796 (git diff): same keyframe select rule; same tokens -> bilinear upsample -> PCA -> unit path (tokens kept as fp32 on the CPU); CSS text still built from the same PCA and templates before the extractor is freed.

baselines_state/load_baselines/row_factory round trip on the real val checkpoints: NormLift(with_averaging=True), ViewCount(feature_from=0) rewired to the NormLift feature, CSS(text 24x64, class_ids). Every uncertainty channel is finite; C_inter <= 1 up to float error.
Averaging, NormLift and view count share one buffer. Their separate beta fits came out identical (36.0027), with identical metrics, as the paper's 'same predictive as averaging' claims.

The tie rule, coverage rule, NLL temperature fit (BetaFitter; init 1 for probs rows, 10 for feature rows) and ABSENT_SCORE pooling across val scenes treat probs rows (CSS) and feature rows the same way. I found no artefact there behind CSS's ECE.
make_tables.py maps each Table I row to the channel the caption names: normlift_1-R, normlift_1-Cinter, css_var_top, and u_ale for ours; '--' for 2D and averaging; OV cross only for CSS.
Yager fusion (baselines.py:298-302) is correct: conflict k = (sum b)(sum b') - sum b_c b'_c goes to ignorance, and an empty view (b = 0, u = 1) is the identity.
View count (n_vis: m > 0; n_full: m >= a0*H*W, the same ref as the field) is computed but appears in no paper table or figure, so its definition affects no reported number.
The 2D row uses the same tokens -> upsample -> the map's PCA path and the same label grid as mapping, and gets its own val beta (33.48).
